cells.quote: This resulted in a higher learning gain throughout sessions 1 to 5 in the Met group, reﬂected by a higher amplitude in the exponential and a higher slope in the linear model compared to theVal group, respectively. This effect was most pronounced in thepracticedcondition.

O.outcome_detail: error rates during the procedural working-memory task

cells.quote: The linear parameter estimates m and the exponential decay constants τ were all negative, indicating a reduction in error rates across sessions, as expected (see Table 1).
cells.note: The study reports that exponential learning curves fit better than linear curves for all task conditions.

O.outcome_detail: functional brain activation, including fronto-striatal regions

cells.quote: We show that repeated training led to an exponential decay in a distributed set of brain regions including fronto-striatal circuits, which paralleled the exponential improvement in task performance.
cells.note: The study reports activation decay as a neural marker of learning and automatization, but the coding scheme does not define higher or lower activation as intrinsically better.

O.outcome_detail: error rates and learning trajectory in the procedural working-memory task

cells.quote: In line with previous studies targeting declarative memory36, risk allele carriers showed an overall higher level of error rates and protracted learning.
cells.note: The study identifies Met-allele carriers as risk-allele carriers; genotype was measured rather than randomly assigned.

O.outcome_detail: genotype-specific trajectories of functional activation in frontal, striatal and thalamic regions

cells.quote: This pattern of BDNF-related differences in behavior is most closely reflected by signal decay curves in frontal cortical areas which demonstrate much stronger activation in risk-allele carriers in the first session but similar activation levels by the end of training (convergence). Striatal and thalamic areas, in contrast, tend to show an oppositive pattern with protracted deactivation in risk-allele carriers and an increasing divergence of BDNF-groups throughout learning.
cells.note: Across 246 parcels, 23 regions showed genotype differences in exponential-curve goodness of fit; the regional activation trajectories differed in direction and pattern.

O.outcome_detail: L-LTP, measured by fEPSP slope 3 h after l-TBS

cells.quote: Application of BDNF 60 min before to 5 min after l-TBS failed to rescue L-LTP in BDNF+/ − (control) slices (Figure 1a). Field excitatory postsynaptic potential (fEPSP) measured 3 h after l-TBS in control 101.8 ± 8.6% of baseline, but 115.5 ± 12.7% in ‘+ BDNF ’ group (Student ’s t-test, P = 0.408).
cells.note: The study describes the non-significant result as a failure to rescue; no equivalence test or adequate-power claim was reported.

O.outcome_detail: L-LTP, measured by fEPSP slope 3 h after l-TBS

cells.quote: Perfusion of tPA (500 ng/ml) at stage I (from 30 min before to 30 min after l-TBS) completely rescued L-LTP (Figure 2a, tPA − / − , 110.4 ± 6.8%; tPA − / − +tPA, 150.3 ± 9.0%, P o0.05), whereas application of tPA at stage II (30 –90 min after l-TBS) failed to restore L-LTP in tPA − / − slices (Figure 2a, tPA − / − , 110.4 ± 6.8%; tPA − / − +tPA, 113.4 ± 12.0%, P = 0.840).
cells.note: The study used genetically deficient mouse hippocampal slices; random assignment was not stated.

O.outcome_detail: L-LTP, measured by fEPSP slope after l-TBS

cells.quote: Application of FIN II (50 μM) to hippocampal slices at stage I had no effect on L-LTP expression (Figure 6d, control, 156.0 ± 7.1%; FIN II, 154.2 ± 17.4%, P = 0.926). However, when applied at stage II, this inhibitor markedly impaired L-LTP within a short period of time (Figure 6e, control, 156.0 ± 7.1%; FIN II, 107.6 ± 10.9%, P o0.05).
cells.note: This supports a maintenance-stage requirement for intracellular proBDNF cleavage by FIN/PC1; learner expertise and participant age were not stated.

O.outcome_detail: late-phase long-term potentiation measured 3 h after l-TBS

cells.quote: Application of the protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin (40 μM) throughout the recording completely prevented L-LTP (Figure 3a). Perfusion of BDNF 60 min before to 5 min after l-TBS could not rescue L-LTP (Figure 3a, anisomycin, 101.4 ± 6.6%; anisomycin +BDNF, 102.6 ± 7.5%, P = 0.885), while BDNF perfused 5-180 min after l-TBS reversed the L-LTP impairment by anisomycin (Figure 3b, anisomycin, 101.4 ± 6.6%; anisomycin+BDNF, 164.5 ± 13.7%, Po 0.005).
cells.note: The study reports field recordings from hippocampal slices; assignment method is not stated.
